Political House of Cards

By: Jane Lipman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
What is going on with South Africa's National Prosecuting Authority? The NDPP position,called the poisoned chalice by some. Carte Blanche looks at why the Cassim Commission was dropped, why the NPA heads never seem to last? Can South Africans trust their key institutions ? Are these institutions still independent ? Or Is there political interference from the president? Carte Blanche interviews, Vusi Pikoli, Judge Johan Kriegler, Lawson Naidoo, Advocate Cassim and we will interview Advocate Abrahams, they new NDPP. We have access to confidential information from a highly placed source in the National Prosecuting Authority.

Further information:
We will interview the Finance Minister Nene, Musi Maimane, a source from the NPA, retired Judge Kriegler, Cassim. We will provide a history of the National Prosecuting Authority. Do all roads lead back to Jacob Zuma , or is the infighting also about internal struggles for power and control? We explain the murky developments ....

Press Release:


NPA: New Blood
Appointed by President Jacob Zuma, new National Director of Public Prosecutions - 39-year-old Advocate Shaun Abrahams - replaces previous head of the NPA, Mxolisi Nxasana who recently left the organisation with a multi-million rand payout. Abrahams this week stressed to media that he would not be using his powers to protect anybody and aspires to fulfil his full term – a feat no other NPA boss has yet achieved. Carte Blanche looks into a state entity dogged by high-level political interference.


Script:


SCRIPT POLITICAL HOUSE OF CARDS – final with Amalia and Wynand.

This week 39 year old Advocate Shaun Abrahams was introduced to media and staff of the National Prosecuting Authority as new Director of Public Prosecutions.

Sound up from Abrahams: “We need to vigorously fight the scourge of corruption and organised crime and serious economic offences. I need each and every one of you to commit to this journey which we will walk together.”

It now rests upon his shoulders to rescue the NPA – started in 1998 - from its controversial and chequered history.

Jane put the dates up -
Over the last seventeen years, none of the NPA Directors of the have served out a full term. The job is seen as a poisoned chalice.
• Bulelani Ngcuka was appointed in 1998 and resigned in 2004.
• Vusi Pikoli took over in 2005 and left three years later even though a high level enquiry found him suitable for office.
• Mokotedi Mpshe acted as National Director until 2009 when Menzi Simelane came until 2012 only to be succeeded by Mxolisi Nxasana. He left the NPA in early June year following a reported R17mn golden handshake.
• In a job where independence is vital, there have been allegations throughout that each NPA head was pressured by political interference.

JOHN LINK Reports of political meddling in the affairs of the National Prosecuting Authority are nothing new. They go back at least as far as when Vusi Pikoli was the National Director of Public Prosecutions. Back then they revolved around his handling of the case against former police commissioner Jackie Selebi and then ANC Deputy President Jacob Zuma.

In a rare television interview Vusi Pikoli agreed to speak to us about his views on the NPA. For him, the NPA’s independence was first called into question at the time of his investigation into corruption allegations against Jackie Selebi.

VUSI PIKOLI: U/S:

The Council for the Advancement of the South African Constitution’s Lawson Naidoo believes that the corruption charges against Zuma were instrumental in Bulenani Ncquka and Vusi Pikoli losing their jobs

Lawson U/S: People speak about current political influence but if one goes back to 2003, the statement by the then NDPP, Bulelani Ncguka, about the fact that whilst there may have been a prima facie case to prosecute against Jacob Zuma, they felt that it was not a winnable case, that was evidence of political influence and interference and political factors, interfering in the NPA’s mandate .

As the head of prosecutions at the time, Vusi Pikoli was looking at charging both Jackie Selebi and President Jacob Zuma with corruption.

I think the immediate reason for my suspension was the Jackie Selebi matter.

But the Zuma matter also compromised his position.

VUSI U/S: I never felt being driven to prosecute Mr Zuma. His prosecution would have been based purely on legal grounds in terms of the evidence. More so that the NPA had won a number of court battles in the question of evidence.

Questions over whether to charge Police Commissioner Selebi and then Deputy President Zuma remained at the time of the ANC Polokwane conference in 2007 where then President Thabo Mbeki and Jacob Zuma battled for power.

President Jacob Zuma has always maintained that the corruption charges from 2003 have been dealt with. NNB: date the Zuma clip.

Zuma U/S: “With regard to the corruption charges, I am not under any charge , I was charged, I went to court to be tried and the State did not have a case to put at the time, and they said they will come back , and I don’t want to speculate about that one , and I think its not right for people to bring this issue when they know I ‘ve got no charges facing me “

After Pikoli’s departure, Moketedi Mpshe came in to the NPA as acting National Director. In April 2009 he dropped the charges against Zuma but recently changed his stance on the matter.

John stand up In a recent court affidavit the former acting head of the NPA Mokedi Mpshe says that had he been able to he would have prosecuted Jacob Zuma before Polokwane in 2007, but he says the only person able to make that call was the former head of the Scorpions Leonard McCarthy. Cut the end of this link out Mpshe famously dropped all charges against Zuma in 2009 citing political interference.

Later that year Moketedi Mpshe left the NPA paving the way for Menzi Simelane who didn’t finish his term in the job either when the Constitutional Court ruled his appointment was invalid.

John standup: We’ve been approached by a high level source with detailed knowledge of the levels of political interference in the functioning of the National Prosecuting Authority. While unwilling to go on camera, the source felt compelled to come to us and explain the extent of the rot.

Our source told us that the ongoing crisis worsened after Menzi Simelane’s departure. Infighting centred around Acting National Prosecutions Chief 42-year-old Advocate Nomgcobo Jiba, a former prosecutor with the Scorpions.

John Webb /link
Our source told me that as a close ally of President Jacob Zuma, Advocate Jiba expected to be appointed head of the National Prosecuting Authority after the departure of Menzi Simelane. Its alleged that her confidence came from her pivotal role in a faction that also included the former head of crime intelligence Richard Mdluli, but Advocate Nxasana was appointed instead. Apparently that led to open warfare between the two .

Jiba’s qualifications are currently under investigation and she faces charges of perjury in relation to her role in the failed prosecution of former Hawks boss Johan Booysens who faced racketeering charges in Kwa Zulu Natal.

Our source revealed two factions in the National Prosecuting Authority - one led by Jiba and the other by Nxasana, with the Jiba camp being closer to President Zuma and Minister in the Presidency Jeff Radebe. New head of the NPA, Advocate Abraham responded in writing that he was unaware of any such factions and investigations into Advocate Jiba are still being considered.

Nxasana himself had an enquiry into his fitness to hold office for various reasons including his having failed to disclose his acquittal in relation to a murder charge he faced in 1986. In early June this year he was given a reported R17 million settlement and left the NPA.

U/S: Abrahams: I am not going to use my position to protect anyone -

Abrahams has now stepped into the pinnacle position in a seemingly frightening network of patronage and infighting.

Abrahams: How do I protect myself from political interference? I am a lawyer and an officer of the court and once again I am going to reiterate that we are bound by the rule of law and the constitution.

Regaining the South Africans public’s confidence in the independence and efficiency of NPA will be no mean feat for Abrahams.

Promo 1: 10 seconds
The job’s been called a poisoned chalice. Can the new head of the National Prosecuting Authority sweep clean?
U/S: I am a lawyer and an officer of the court and once again I am going to reiterate that we are bound by the rule of law and the constitution.

Promo 2: 15 seconds
None of the former heads of the National Prosecuting Authority have managed to serve out a full term. Will new head Advocate Shaun Abrahams be the first?
U/S: I am not going to use my position to protect anyone -

Promo 3: 15 seconds
Can Shaun Abrahams, new head of the National Prosecuting Authority, regain South Africa’s confidence in the organisation’s independence?
U/S: Sound up from Abrahams: “We need to vigorously fight the scourge of corruption and organised crime and serious economic offences.
